exercises.task: Open Data → Data View, then the Variable View tab, and list the numeric/scale vs categorical variables.
exercises.answer: You should see: scale: age, bmi, systolic_bp, cholesterol, pain_score, new_biomarker, followup_months. Categorical: sex, treatment, smoking, outcome, gold_standard, event_death. Why: measurement scale decides which test you can use.

exercises.task: Run descriptive statistics on age, bmi, systolic_bp, cholesterol.
exercises.answer: You should see: for each variable: N, mean, SD, median, min, max, skewness. Why: mean+SD summarise symmetric data; median is better with skew.

exercises.task: Identify which variable is skewed and which is roughly symmetric.
exercises.answer: You should see: age and bmi skewness near 0 (symmetric). Why: skewness ≈ ±0.5 is acceptable; >1 is markedly skewed.

exercises.task: Compare mean vs median for age.
exercises.answer: You should see: mean ≈ median (both ≈ 58). Why: when mean≈median the distribution is symmetric.

exercises.task: Get frequencies for smoking and for treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: counts + % for each category. Why: frequencies summarise categorical data; report n and %.

exercises.task: Describe the distribution of BMI (central tendency + spread + shape).
exercises.answer: You should see: mean ≈ 27, SD ≈ 4.9, median ≈ 27, min 15, max 40, skew ≈ 0.2. Why: roughly normal; report mean (SD).

exercises.task: Find the interquartile range (IQR) equivalent for systolic_bp.
exercises.answer: You should see: Q1 ≈ 89, Q3 ≈ 103 (IQR ≈ 14). Why: IQR is robust to outliers; with skew, report median (IQR).

exercises.task: State whether systolic_bp has outliers.
exercises.answer: You should see: a few points beyond the whiskers. Why: boxplots reveal outliers that would distort the mean.

exercises.task: Classify pain_score (0–10).
exercises.answer: You should see: ordinal (ordered integer scale, not truly continuous). Why: treat ordinal as non-continuous; prefer non-parametric tests.

exercises.task: Report "age" both as mean(SD) and median(IQR) — which fits better?
exercises.answer: You should see: symmetric → mean (SD) is fine. Why: symmetric data: mean (SD); skewed: median (IQR).

exercises.task: Determine which variable is most appropriate to report as a proportion.
exercises.answer: You should see: outcome / smoking → counts + %. Why: binary/categorical → proportions, not mean.

exercises.task: Find the coefficient of variation (CV) of BMI.
exercises.answer: You should see: ≈ 5/27 ≈ 18%. Why: CV standardises spread, useful comparing variables on different scales.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Make a histogram of bmi with a normal curve.
exercises.answer: You should see: bell-shaped with the normal curve close to the bars. Why: normality underpins parametric tests.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Run a Q–Q plot of bmi.
exercises.answer: You should see: points close to the diagonal. Why: Q-Q is a visual normality check.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Run the Shapiro–Wilk test on bmi.
exercises.answer: You should see: p > 0.05 → not significantly non-normal. Why: p > 0.05 means we cannot reject normality.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Estimate the proportion of patients within mean ± 1 SD for age.
exercises.answer: You should see: ≈ 70% fall within mean ± 1 SD. Why: the 68–95–99.7 rule for normal data.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Compute the z-score of a patient aged 78 (mean 58, SD 15).
exercises.answer: You should see: z = (78−57.8)/14.2 ≈ 1.42 → 92nd centile. Why: z tells you how many SDs from the mean.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Explain why sample mean is more reliable than a single observation.
exercises.answer: You should see: the standard error of the mean decreases as n grows. Why: SE = SD/√n — the CLT makes means normal even if data aren't.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Check normality of systolic_bp.
exercises.answer: You should see: near-normal (p > 0.05). Why: OK for parametric tests on the mean.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Explain why you can still use a t-test on a slightly non-normal variable with n=240.
exercises.answer: You should see: with large n the sample mean is approximately normal. Why: the Central Limit Theorem justifies parametric tests on means for large samples.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Check whether pain_score is normally distributed — and say why that matters.
exercises.answer: You should see: transformed/ordinal → not normal. Why: ordinal data → use non-parametric tests.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: State the standard error of the mean for bmi.
exercises.answer: You should see: SD/√n ≈ 5/√240 ≈ 0.32. Why: SE measures how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean.

exercises.topic: Normal distribution & the Central Limit Theorem
exercises.task: Draw the 68/95/99.7 boundaries for bmi.
exercises.answer: You should see: 22–32 (68%), 17–37 (95%), 12–42 (99.7%). Why: the rule-of-thumb spread for normal data.

exercises.task: Get the mean and 95% CI of systolic_bp by treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: three means (≈94–100) each with a 95% CI. Why: a 95% CI is the range likely to contain the true mean.

exercises.task: Interpret two overlapping CIs.
exercises.answer: You should see: overlapping CIs suggest no statistically significant difference. Why: overlap implies the difference may be due to chance.

exercises.task: Identify where the 95% CI excludes the null (a difference of 0) between treatments.
exercises.answer: You should see: Drug B–Placebo CIs barely overlap / difference CI excludes 0. Why: when the difference's CI excludes 0, p < 0.05 typically.

exercises.task: Compute a 95% CI for the mean of bmi.
exercises.answer: You should see: mean ≈ 27.1, 95% CI ≈ 26.5–27.7. Why: 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SE.

exercises.task: State the null and alternative hypothesis for "does treatment affect systolic_bp?"
exercises.answer: You should see: H₀: no difference between groups; H₁: a difference exists. Why: hypothesis testing starts from the null.

exercises.task: Explain what a p-value < 0.05 means (and what it does NOT).
exercises.answer: You should see: the probability of the data if the null were true; it is not the probability the null is true. Why: common misinterpretation — p is not "5% chance the result is wrong".

exercises.task: Define a Type I error.
exercises.answer: You should see: rejecting a true null (false positive); risk = α. Why: α = 0.05 → 5% chance of a false positive.

exercises.task: Define a Type II error and state power.
exercises.answer: You should see: failing to detect a true effect (false negative); power = 1−β. Why: power is the chance of detecting a real difference.

exercises.task: Explain the relationship between CI width and sample size.
exercises.answer: You should see: bigger n → smaller SE → narrower CI. Why: CI narrows as √n grows.

exercises.task: State when you would use a one-tailed test.
exercises.answer: You should see: only when a directional (one-sided) hypothesis is justified pre-specified. Why: one-tailed gives more power but demands a strong a priori direction.

exercises.task: Interpret a result with p = 0.06: significant or not?
exercises.answer: You should see: not significant at α=0.05, but report the exact p (and CI) rather than just "NS". Why: avoid the "p-hacking" dichotomisation; report uncertainty.

exercises.task: Run an independent t-test: BMI by sex.
exercises.path: Analyze → Compare Means (Test type: Independent t-test)
exercises.answer: You should see: Levene test + t-test; p ≈ 0.69 → no significant difference. Why: p > 0.05 → fail to reject H₀.

exercises.task: Read Levene's test and say which t-test to use.
exercises.path: Analyze → Compare Means (Test type: Independent t-test)
exercises.answer: You should see: Levene p > 0.05 → equal variances → Student's t. Why: if variances differ, use Welch's t.

exercises.task: Run a one-way ANOVA: systolic_bp by treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: F ≈ 7.0, p ≈ 0.001 → significant. Why: at least one group differs. ANOVA doesn't tell you which.

exercises.task: Read the Tukey post-hoc after a significant ANOVA.
exercises.answer: You should see: Drug B–Placebo significantly different (p < 0.05). Why: post-hoc adjusts for multiple comparisons.

exercises.task: State why you cannot run three separate t-tests instead of an ANOVA + post-hoc.
exercises.answer: You should see: multiple testing inflates the Type I error. Why: correction (Tukey/Bonferroni) controls the family-wise error.

exercises.task: Run a paired t-test comparing systolic vs diastolic BP.
exercises.path: Analyze → Compare Means (Test type: Paired t-test)
exercises.answer: You should see: a clearly significant difference (p < 0.001). Why: paired measures on the same patient remove between-subject variability.

exercises.task: Explain the difference between paired and independent t-tests.
exercises.answer: You should see: paired = same subjects twice (more power); independent = separate groups. Why: use the design to choose the test.

exercises.task: Check the assumptions for the independent t-test you ran.
exercises.answer: You should see: each group near-normal and equal variances. Why: t-test assumes normality + homoscedasticity.

exercises.task: Compute the effect size (Cohen's d) for BMI male vs female.
exercises.answer: You should see: d ≈ 0.05 (tiny). Why: a non-significant result with tiny effect — report effect size, not just p.

exercises.task: Run a two-way ANOVA with two factors and interpret interaction.
exercises.answer: You should see: main effects + interaction term. Why: interaction = whether the effect of one factor depends on the other.

exercises.task: State when to use a one-sample t-test.
exercises.answer: You should see: comparing a sample mean to a known reference value. Why: e.g. is our mean BP different from 120?

exercises.task: Summarise the outcome of testing BMI by sex in one sentence.
exercises.answer: You should see: "No significant difference in BMI between sexes (t=…, p=0.69, d=0.06)." Why: the clinical takeaway is a null result.

exercises.task: Run a chi-square test: treatment × outcome.
exercises.answer: You should see: χ² with p < 0.001 → association. Why: improvement depends on treatment.

exercises.task: Check the minimum expected count — would Fisher's exact be needed?
exercises.answer: You should see: all expected counts > 5 → chi-square OK. Why: Fisher's exact is for small/sparse tables (expected < 5).

exercises.task: Run Fisher's exact on sex × smoking.
exercises.answer: You should see: Fisher exact p — likely non-significant. Why: exact test for 2×2 small tables.

exercises.task: Run the Mann–Whitney U test on pain_score by sex.
exercises.answer: You should see: U statistic + p. Why: ranks — for non-normal/ordinal data between two groups.

exercises.task: Run Wilcoxon signed-rank on pain_score vs a paired ordinal measure.
exercises.answer: You should see: a rank-based paired test p. Why: the non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test.

exercises.task: Run Kruskal–Wallis on pain_score by treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: H statistic + p. Why: non-parametric one-way ANOVA.

exercises.task: Run the Sign Test on a paired binary/ordinal change.
exercises.answer: You should see: counts of +/− differences and a sign-test p. Why: the non-parametric test for paired (before/after) data — like McNemar for binary outcomes.

exercises.task: Run the binomial test on sex (test proportion 0.5).
exercises.answer: You should see: compares observed proportion to 0.5; p ≈ 0.9 → balanced. Why: tests whether a binary proportion differs from a set value.

exercises.task: Run the runs test on age.
exercises.answer: You should see: tests randomness of the sequence. Why: checks for non-random patterns.

exercises.task: Run the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test on bmi.
exercises.answer: You should see: p > 0.05 → consistent with normal. Why: an alternative normality test (less powerful than Shapiro).

exercises.task: Run the Friedman test on three related ordinal measures.
exercises.answer: You should see: the non-parametric repeated-measures ANOVA. Why: for matched/related groups of 3+.

exercises.task: Run Pearson correlation between age and systolic_bp.
exercises.answer: You should see: r ≈ 0.7, p < 0.001 → strong positive. Why: older patients have higher systolic BP.

exercises.task: Run Spearman correlation between age and pain_score.
exercises.answer: You should see: ρ for ranked/ordinal data. Why: Spearman for non-normal/ordinal or monotonic relationships.

exercises.task: Interpret r² for age–systolic_bp.
exercises.answer: You should see: r² ≈ 0.48 → 48% of BP variance explained. Why: r² is the proportion of shared variance.

exercises.task: Build a correlation matrix of age, bmi, systolic_bp, cholesterol.
exercises.answer: You should see: a 4×4 matrix with r + p for each pair. Why: screening for associations; watch for multiple testing.

exercises.task: Run simple linear regression: systolic_bp ~ age.
exercises.answer: You should see: coefficient ≈ 0.47 mmHg/yr, p < 0.001, R² ≈ 0.48. Why: each extra year adds ~0.5 mmHg.

exercises.task: Run multiple linear regression: systolic_bp ~ age + bmi + cholesterol.
exercises.answer: You should see: adjusted model summary + coefficients. Why: adjusts each predictor for the others.

exercises.task: Interpret the age coefficient in the multiple model.
exercises.answer: You should see: age still significant (p < 0.001), coefficient slightly reduced. Why: the effect is adjusted for BMI and cholesterol.

exercises.task: Check the LINE assumptions of your linear regression.
exercises.answer: You should see: residual vs fit roughly random; residuals ~normal. Why: LINE: Linear, Independent, Normal, Equal-variances errors.

exercises.task: Compare adjusted R² to R² in the multiple model.
exercises.answer: You should see: adjusted R² slightly lower than R². Why: adjusted R² penalises adding unhelpful predictors.

exercises.task: Identify why you should check for multicollinearity (VIF) before interpreting beta weights.
exercises.answer: You should see: highly correlated predictors destabilise coefficients (VIF > 5–10). Why: cannot separate the individual effects.

exercises.task: Interpret the intercept in the systolic_bp ~ age model.
exercises.answer: You should see: intercept ≈ predicted BP at age 0 (extrapolation, not meaningful clinically). Why: intercepts can be out of the observed range.

exercises.task: Run logistic regression: outcome ~ age + bmi + treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: a fitted model with coefficients, ORs, p-values. Why: models the log-odds of "not improved".

exercises.task: Interpret the odds ratio for treatment (active vs placebo).
exercises.answer: You should see: OR < 1 for active treatment → lower odds of the negative outcome. Why: OR < 1 = protective.

exercises.task: Interpret the OR for age.
exercises.answer: You should see: OR per year — likely > 1 (older → worse). Why: OR is per 1-unit increase.

exercises.task: Read the 95% CI of an odds ratio and decide significance.
exercises.answer: You should see: CI excluding 1 → significant. Why: OR null value is 1; CI excluding 1 = significant.

exercises.task: Explain what MLE produces in logistic regression.
exercises.answer: You should see: coefficients that maximise the likelihood of the observed data. Why: logistic uses MLE, not least squares.

exercises.task: Explain pseudo-R² (e.g. McFadden).
exercises.answer: You should see: a rough measure of model fit (not comparable to linear R²). Why: used with caution — compare models, don't quote as % explained.

exercises.task: Interpret the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test.
exercises.answer: You should see: p > 0.05 → adequate fit. Why: tests calibration across risk deciles.

exercises.task: Check AIC/BIC to compare two logistic models.
exercises.answer: You should see: lower AIC/BIC → better (parsimonious) model. Why: penalises complexity.

exercises.task: Explain the events-per-variable (EPV) rule of thumb.
exercises.answer: You should see: ≥10 events per predictor to avoid overfitting. Why: too many predictors → unstable estimates.

exercises.task: State when to use multinomial vs ordinal logistic.
exercises.answer: You should see: >2 unordered categories → multinomial; ordered → ordinal (proportional odds). Why: use the outcome structure.

exercises.task: Compute the probability of "Not improved" overall.
exercises.answer: You should see: ≈ 42%. Why: the baseline risk of the event.

exercises.task: Compute the risk of "Not improved" in Placebo vs Drug A.
exercises.answer: You should see: Placebo higher risk than Drug A. Why: risk = events/total in each arm.

exercises.task: Compute the relative risk (RR) of Drug A vs Placebo.
exercises.answer: You should see: RR = risk(A)/risk(Placebo) < 1. Why: RR < 1 = reduced risk with treatment.

exercises.task: Compute the odds ratio of the same comparison.
exercises.answer: You should see: OR < 1 and roughly similar to RR (common outcome → OR exaggerates). Why: OR and RR diverge when the event is common.

exercises.task: Compute the absolute risk reduction (ARR) and NNT.
exercises.answer: You should see: ARR = risk diff; NNT = 1/ARR. Why: NNT = number needed to treat for one benefit.

exercises.task: Run a diagnostic test: new_biomarker vs gold_standard.
exercises.answer: You should see: 2×2 table with sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy. Why: quantifies test accuracy against a reference.

exercises.task: Interpret the sensitivity and specificity you obtained.
exercises.answer: You should see: sensitivity = TPR (catches disease); specificity = TNR (rules out). Why: sensitivity/specificity are properties of the test itself.

exercises.task: Explain how PPV changes with disease prevalence.
exercises.answer: You should see: PPV rises with prevalence; NPV falls. Why: PPV depends on the pre-test probability.

exercises.task: Run an ROC curve for new_biomarker and read the AUC.
exercises.answer: You should see: AUC ≈ 0.78 → good discrimination. Why: 0.5 = chance; >0.8 = excellent.

exercises.task: Explain how to pick the optimal cut-off from the ROC.
exercises.answer: You should see: maximise (sens + spec − 1) → top-left point. Why: balances sensitivity and specificity.

exercises.task: Compute the positive likelihood ratio (LR+).
exercises.answer: You should see: LR+ > 1 (ideally >5). Why: how much a positive test increases the odds of disease.

exercises.task: Run Kaplan–Meier: followup_months by treatment.
exercises.vars: time: followup_months; status: event_death; factor: treatment
exercises.answer: You should see: three survival curves, median survival, log-rank test. Why: KM estimates survival over time.

exercises.task: Read the median survival for each treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: Drug A longest, Placebo shortest median. Why: median survival = time to 50% survival.

exercises.task: Read the log-rank p-value and interpret.
exercises.answer: You should see: log-rank p < 0.05 → survival differs between groups. Why: log-rank compares the whole survival curve.

exercises.task: Explain censoring in the data.
exercises.answer: You should see: vertical tick marks = censored (event_death=0). Why: a subject is censored if the event hasn't happened by the end of follow-up.

exercises.task: Run Cox proportional hazards: event ~ age + bmi + treatment.
exercises.answer: You should see: hazard ratios with 95% CIs and p-values. Why: Cox models the hazard (instantaneous risk).

exercises.task: Interpret the hazard ratio for active treatment vs placebo.
exercises.answer: You should see: HR < 1 → lower hazard (protective). Why: HR < 1 = reduced risk of the event.

exercises.task: Interpret the HR for age.
exercises.answer: You should see: HR > 1 per year → older patients have higher hazard. Why: HR is per unit increase.

exercises.task: State the proportional hazards assumption.
exercises.answer: You should see: the HR is constant over time; check with Schoenfeld residuals. Why: if violated, a time-dependent model is needed.

exercises.task: Explain the difference between Kaplan–Meier and Cox.
exercises.answer: You should see: KM = descriptive curves + log-rank; Cox = multivariable hazard ratios. Why: Cox lets you adjust for covariates.

exercises.task: Explain competing risks and when the Fine–Gray model is used.
exercises.answer: You should see: when an event prevents the event of interest (e.g. death vs recurrence). Why: standard KM overestimates when competing events exist.

exercises.task: Explain why the survival curve at the far right tail may be unstable.
exercises.answer: You should see: few subjects remain at risk → wide CI / unreliable. Why: small numbers at risk at the end.

exercises.task: Run a power analysis for an independent t-test (d=0.5, power=0.8).
exercises.path: Analyze → Power Analysis (Test: Independent t-test (2 groups); ask: How many patients do I need?)
exercises.answer: You should see: ≈64 per group (≈128 total). Why: standard sample size for a medium effect.

exercises.task: Run power for a Paired t-test (d=0.5) and compare to the independent t-test.
exercises.path: Analyze → Power Analysis (Test: Paired t-test (before/after); ask: How many patients do I need?)
exercises.answer: You should see: fewer "patients" than the independent t-test for the same effect. Why: a paired design uses each subject as their own control, so it needs a smaller sample for the same power.

exercises.task: Run power for a one-way ANOVA (f=0.25, 3 groups).
exercises.answer: You should see: a total sample size for 80% power. Why: ANOVA needs more subjects as groups increase.

exercises.task: Explain how sample size changes as alpha shrinks.
exercises.answer: You should see: smaller α (e.g. 0.01) → larger n. Why: stricter significance needs more data.

exercises.task: Explain intention-to-treat (ITT) vs per-protocol.
exercises.answer: You should see: ITT = analyse as randomised; PP = only those who completed. Why: ITT is the primary, unbiased analysis.

exercises.task: State the purpose of blinding and randomisation.
exercises.answer: You should see: randomisation removes allocation bias; blinding reduces bias in assessment. Why: strengthen causal inference.

exercises.task: Explain a non-inferiority trial.
exercises.answer: You should see: shows the new treatment is no worse than control within a margin. Why: bounds the difference, not just equivalence.

exercises.task: Explain the multiple-comparisons problem and how to correct it.
exercises.answer: You should see: more tests → more false positives; correct with Bonferroni/FDR. Why: controls the family-wise or false-discovery rate.

exercises.task: Explain confounding and how to address it.
exercises.answer: You should see: a third variable distorts the association; adjust via stratification/regression/randomisation. Why: confounders create spurious associations.

exercises.task: Explain Simpson's paradox with an example.
exercises.answer: You should see: a trend reverses when data are grouped. Why: confounding by a hidden group.

exercises.task: List the main types of bias in observational studies.
exercises.answer: You should see: selection, recall, information, confounding. Why: recognise and design to minimise them.

exercises.task: Explain the difference between statistical and clinical significance.
exercises.answer: You should see: p<0.05 ≠ clinically important; look at effect size + CI. Why: a tiny statistically significant effect may not matter in practice.
